title: Two different classifications

blocks.heading: Two different classifications
blocks.text: Employment status concerns whether and how much someone works; formal or informal economic activity concerns institutional and regulatory arrangements. An informal economic activity is not an informal settlement, which describes a residential area; neither label alone determines a person’s employment status. A person can work in a registered business while living in an informal settlement. Another can carry out informal economic work elsewhere. Test whether the evidence describes work, registration or housing. The classifications can be combined rather than substituted for each other.
context_tags: original teaching; fictional examples where stated

blocks.heading: Unemployment and underemployment
blocks.text: Unemployment is the situation of people without work who are available for and seeking work; exact statistical definitions depend on the source. Underemployment means having work that uses less than a person’s available working time or productive capacity; it differs from having no work. An invented worker seeking work but with no job is distinguished from a worker with six paid hours who is available for more. State what is measured; not everyone without a job is counted as unemployed, for example if unavailable for work under the stated definition. A low-hours example illustrates time-related underemployment without claiming that every part-time worker is underemployed.
context_tags: original teaching; fictional examples where stated

blocks.heading: Formal and informal sector
blocks.text: Formal economic activity operates within the relevant recognised registration and regulatory arrangements; informal activity operates outside some of them. The exact statistical boundary depends on the source; informal does not by itself mean unemployed, illegal or located in an informal settlement. An invented unregistered repair activity still produces a service and can provide work and income. Its institutional classification says nothing by itself about the quality of the worker’s home. A registered shop may also offer few hours, so formal status does not establish adequate employment. Use the definition and relevant evidence together.
context_tags: original teaching; fictional examples where stated

blocks.heading: An original work comparison
blocks.text: In a fictional survey of 100 people available for and seeking more work, 30 have no work, 40 have fewer paid hours than they are available for, and 30 have their desired hours. The no-work and insufficient-hours groups together show a shortfall in work, but 70 have some employment. Calling all 70 people with unmet work needs unemployed would erase the distinction. A separate registration table could classify their economic activities; their housing location would not answer it. Topic 3.1 explains labour as a productive input; here classify work status and activity correctly.
context_tags: original teaching; fictional examples where stated

blocks.heading: Connect causes and responses
blocks.text: Keep work, institutional registration and residential location separate. An informal settlement can contain people in different work situations.
